cards.title: Introduction to Control Flow and Decision Making
cards.content:
Control flow statements break up the flow of execution by employing decision-making, looping, and branching mechanisms, enabling your program to conditionally execute blocks of code.

The most basic decision-making statement is if-else:

int score = 85;
if (score >= 90) {
    System.out.println("Grade: A");
} else if (score >= 80) {
    System.out.println("Grade: B");
} else {
    System.out.println("Grade: C");
}

Java evaluates conditions from top to bottom. Once a condition evaluates to true, its block runs, and the remaining statements are bypassed.

cards.title: The Ternary Operator
cards.content:
The ternary operator is a shorthand way of writing an if-else statement that yields a value. It is the only operator in Java that takes three operands.

Syntax:

variable = (condition) ? expressionIfTrue : expressionIfFalse;

Example:

int time = 20;
String greeting = (time < 18) ? "Good day" : "Good evening";
System.out.println(greeting); // Prints "Good evening"

cards.title: Switch Statements & Expressions
cards.content:
A switch statement allows you to test a variable for equality against a list of values. Traditional switch statements require a break statement to prevent falling through to subsequent blocks.

Modern Java (Java 14+) introduced Switch Expressions, which can return a value and use the arrow (->) syntax to eliminate the need for manual break statements:

int numLetters = switch (day) {
    case MONDAY, FRIDAY, SUNDAY -> 6;
    case TUESDAY                -> 7;
    case THURSDAY, SATURDAY     -> 8;
    case WEDNESDAY              -> 9;
    default -> throw new IllegalStateException("Invalid day: " + day);
};

If a multi-line block is required inside a Switch Expression, use the keyword yield to return the value.

cards.title: While vs Do-While Loops
cards.content:
Loops repeat a block of statements while a boolean condition remains true.

  • while loop: Evaluates the condition before executing the loop body (Entry-controlled).
  • do-while loop: Evaluates the condition after executing the loop body (Exit-controlled).
// While Loop
int count = 0;
while (count < 3) {
    System.out.print(count + " ");
    count++;
}

// Do-While Loop
int num = 5;
do {
    System.out.print(num + " ");
    num++;
} while (num < 5);

cards.title: For Loops: Traditional & Enhanced
cards.content:
Java provides two main styles of for loops:

1. Traditional For Loop

Used when you need to track the loop counter or control the step increment.

for (int i = 0; i < 5; i += 2) {
    System.out.print(i + " "); // Prints 0 2 4
}

2. Enhanced For Loop (For-Each)

Used to iterate sequentially through elements of arrays or Collections without index tracking.

String[] fruits = {"Apple", "Banana", "Cherry"};
for (String fruit : fruits) {
    System.out.print(fruit + " ");
}

cards.title: Branching: Break and Continue
cards.content:
Branching statements interrupt sequential execution flow inside loops.

  • break: Immediately terminates the innermost looping structure and transfers execution to the statement following the loop.
  • continue: Skips the remaining statements in the current iteration and evaluates the loop condition for the next pass.
for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
    if (i == 3) {
        continue; // skip 3
    }
    if (i == 5) {
        break; // stop loop before printing 5
    }
    System.out.print(i + " "); // Prints 1 2 4
}

cards.title: Control Flow Best Practices
cards.content:
Writing clean control flow logic prevents cognitive overload and maintains codebase health.

Key Best Practices:

  • Avoid Deep Nesting: Too many nested if-else or loop blocks make code unreadable. Use early exit (Guard Clauses) instead.
  • Prefer Switch Expressions over nested If-Else: Modern switch structures are expressive, easy to read, and verify exhaustiveness.
  • Keep Loop Iterations simple: If loop bodies exceed 15 lines of code, refactor loop logic into clear helper methods.
